1. Validate the current bill: confirm meter reads imply 1,191 kWh (50,037 − 48,846), line items sum to $218.60 ($18.79 + $41.42 + $158.39), and the change versus last month is +$73.49 ($218.60 − $145.11); treat any arithmetic mismatch as a suspected billing error.

2. Map both billing periods to the AEP Ohio tariff: last month (2026-05-25 to 2026-06-23) and the current period (2026-06-23 to 2026-07-28) both fall entirely under the post-2026-04-10 tariff (fixed $18.788; tier-1 variable $0.0347738 + $0.13299 = $0.1677638/kWh for the first 2,000 kWh), so no boundary proration is needed.

3. Set days_usd from the billing-period length difference: current is 35 days versus last month’s 29 days (+6 days), valued at the effective daily cost under the current tariff and usage pattern.

4. Estimate weather_usd from NOAA degree days: compare last month (CDD 158 / HDD 6) to current (CDD 430.5 / HDD 0), derive a weather-to-kWh coefficient from the household’s bill history (e.g., prior summer cooling periods), convert the weather-driven kWh difference to dollars at the effective rate, or set weather_usd = 0 if no defensible coefficient can be estimated.

5. Compute price_usd from any tariff/rate changes applied to baseline usage (effectively $0 here since both periods use the same tariff), compute usage_usd from the 438 kWh increase (753 → 1,191) valued at the effective rate, then set usage_usd as the residual so price_usd + days_usd + weather_usd + usage_usd equals exactly +$73.49.

6. Check for a billing error by comparing the tariff-modeled current-period total to the actual $218.60; if the difference exceeds rounding, set billing_error_suspected = true and billing_error_usd to the discrepancy, otherwise false and null. Return only the JSON object with keys price_usd, days_usd, weather_usd, usage_usd, billing_error_suspected, and billing_error_usd.
